topic: Philosophical and foundational remarks: a chess analogy, Germany's lead in the theory of number from Dedekind and Cantor's dispute with Kronecker, a relative-consistency formulation of Zermelo's axiom of choice, and the relativity of 'working hypothesis' versus 'real existence' with reference to Planck.

triage.modern_statement: This isn't a mathematical research question. The fragment is a rhetorical, epistemological aside: something (probably an entity such as atoms, or a hypothesis in general) is 'in itself only a fantasy. Why?' It sits in Hilbert's remarks on how the line between a 'working hypothesis' and 'real existence' is relative, with reference to Planck. That fits the Planck–Mach debate of 1908–1910 over whether atoms are real or just useful fictions. The subject of the sentence is cut off ('sich nur eine Phantasie'), so the exact referent can't be recovered.
triage.answered_by: Not applicable. It's a philosophical remark, not a problem to be solved. The background debate it seems to point to, Planck's realism against Mach's instrumentalism about atoms, is usually described as having been settled in favour of the reality of atoms by the experimental work of about 1908–1913 (e.g. Perrin). My searches didn't link Hilbert's note to that specifically, so this is context, not an answer to the note.

evidence.claim: Planck set out his epistemological credo in the 1908 Leiden lecture 'Die Einheit des physikalischen Weltbildes', which started his polemic with Mach.
The Planck–Mach controversy was a clash between instrumentalist and realist philosophies of science, centred on whether atoms exist.
Mach and his followers warned against treating entities that had never been observed, such as atoms, as real.

Why?' read as a rhetorical question in that philosophy-of-science discussion (realism against fictionalism or instrumentalism, as in the Planck–Mach dispute). They don't pose a mathematical problem. It doesn't match any of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. Because the subject of the sentence is missing, I can't be sure what Hilbert called a fantasy, and the link to the atom debate is an inference from context rather than something a source confirms. The general realism question is still debated in philosophy of science, but that isn't a mathematical research area tied to this note.
